title: Renal and hepatic routes of elimination

segs.text: Module four, objective one. The main routes by which drugs leave the body, renal and hepatic. Elimination is the irreversible removal of drug from the body, by every route at once. Drug that moves into tissue and later comes back has only been distributed, so distribution is not elimination. There are two ways out. Excretion removes the drug intact, with no chemical change. Biotransformation, also called drug metabolism, converts the drug chemically into a metabolite.

card.m: distribution: drug comes back, not eliminated
excretion: drug removed intact, mainly by the kidney
biotransformation (metabolism): drug → metabolite, mainly in the liver

segs.text: In general, which route a drug takes depends on how well it dissolves in water. The textbook explains that water-soluble drugs are eliminated more rapidly through the kidney, which excretes them into the urine. Many lipid-soluble drugs are metabolized in the liver into more polar, water-soluble metabolites, which the kidney or the bile then excretes. So biotransformation most often produces a compound the body can eliminate more readily than the parent drug. The kidney and the liver are the two major elimination organs: the kidney excretes drug, and the liver biotransforms it.

card.m: lipid-soluble drug → liver → water-soluble metabolite → urine or bile
metabolite: eliminated more readily than the parent drug

segs.text: Each route has its own clearance, the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. Each organ's elimination rate is its clearance times the same plasma concentration, so the rates add, and so do the clearances, to the total body clearance. Cl T equals Cl R plus Cl H, where Cl R is renal clearance and Cl H is hepatic clearance, also called metabolic clearance. A Cl written with no subscript means total body clearance. Because the parts add, a fall in one route lowers the total only by that route's share. In a textbook example, renal clearance is ten and nonrenal five liters per hour; when renal function halves, the total falls from fifteen to ten liters per hour, by one third, not by one half.

card.m: clearance: volume of plasma cleared of drug per time, e.g. L/hr
one route falls → Cl<sub>T</sub> falls by that route's share only
e.g. (textbook) ClR 10 → 5 L/hr, nonrenal 5 L/hr: ClT 15 → 10 L/hr, down ⅓

segs.text: Hepatic clearance is found by difference. The rate and extent of metabolism can rarely be measured directly, and the liver is not sampled, so hepatic clearance is what is left once renal clearance is taken from the total. The second form uses f e, the fraction of the dose recovered unchanged in the urine, which has no units. f e is the kidney's share of the clearance, so one minus f e is the share that is not renal. Cl H equals one minus f e, times Cl T. The larger f e is, the smaller the hepatic part, and the two forms give the same answer.

card.m: f<sub>e</sub>: fraction excreted unchanged, no units
1 − f<sub>e</sub>: the share that is not renal
f<sub>e</sub> up → Cl<sub>H</sub> down, at the same Cl<sub>T</sub>

segs.text: In the worked example, a drug has a total body clearance of one point three liters per hour, and six tenths of the dose is excreted unchanged in the urine. Hepatic clearance is asked, and the form with f e answers it, because f e and the total are both given. Hepatic clearance comes out at zero point five two liters per hour. As a check, renal clearance is zero point seven eight liters per hour, and the total minus that gives the same zero point five two. So the liver accounts for four tenths of this drug's clearance, and the kidney for six tenths.

In her quizzes the routes are asked as vocabulary. Quiz three asked which term describes the process by which drug is chemically converted in the body, and the key is biotransformation, not distribution, excretion or absorption. Two features decide such items: whether the removal is irreversible, which distribution is not, and whether the drug is chemically changed or removed intact. A usual trap swaps the organs, putting excretion in the liver and biotransformation in the kidney. Her review poll stated that hepatic clearance is most readily approximated with creatinine clearance, and the key is false: creatinine clearance estimates the patient's kidney function, and hepatic clearance is total minus renal. Objective five uses these same lines to split a total clearance into its renal and hepatic parts.

card.m: ✗ excretion in the liver, biotransformation in the kidney
objective 5: Cl<sub>R</sub> = f<sub>e</sub> × Cl<sub>T</sub>, Cl<sub>H</sub> = the rest
